title: Inside the Corporation Called Indsco
text:
In the 1970s the sociologist Rosabeth Moss Kanter spent several years studying a large American industrial company, which she called Indsco to protect its identity. She interviewed and observed managers, salespeople, secretaries and the wives of executives, and read company documents, to understand how life inside a big corporation shaped people.

Kanter argued that much of what people attributed to individual personality or to gender was really produced by the structure of their jobs. People whose jobs offered little chance of promotion tended to lower their aspirations, focus on friendships and complain, while those on promising paths became ambitious and engaged. Managers who lacked real power to get resources for their people tended to become controlling and petty.

Her best known analysis concerned what she called tokens: members of a group who make up a small minority, such as the few women among the company's sales force. Because they were so visible, every action was noticed and taken to represent their whole group. Differences between them and the majority were exaggerated, and they were pushed into stereotyped roles. Kanter argued that any minority in such a position would face the same pressures.
lesson: Before blaming people for how they behave, look at the position they hold: their opportunities, their power and whether they are the only one of their kind.
source: Kanter, R. M. (1977). Men and Women of the Corporation. Basic Books.
caveat: It is a case study of a single company, and later research found that men in token positions often do not face the same disadvantages as women.
